steps.body: One piece of an equally-cut whole is a UNIT fraction: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4. The bottom number names how many pieces the whole became.
steps.narration: One piece of an equally-cut whole is a UNIT fraction: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4. The bottom number names how many pieces the whole became.

widget.prompt: Build the unit fraction 1/6: one piece of a whole cut into six.
widget.successFeedback: 1/6 — the whole became six equal pieces and you are holding exactly one.
widget.lowFeedback: Your shaded bar is shorter than the target half. Shade more — raise the numerator, or use fewer parts.
widget.highFeedback: Your shaded bar is longer than half. Shade less — lower the numerator, or split into more parts.

commonFractions.feedback: 1/4 cuts the whole into four bigger pieces. Six pieces means each is smaller.
6/6 shades every piece — that is the whole, not one piece of it.

predict.prompt: Same whole, cut into 3 versus cut into 6. Which pieces are bigger?
predict.reveal: The whole is fixed, so more cuts means smaller pieces — thirds are bigger than sixths.

cml.actionGoal: Cut, count, and compare equal pieces to see what g3f unit name really names.
invariants: A fraction names equal shares of ONE whole: the denominator says how many equal pieces the whole became, and the numerator counts them, which is what makes g3f unit name comparable at all.
misconceptions: Calling unequal pieces fractions, reading the denominator as a count, or comparing fractions that came from different-sized wholes.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the whole changed size, which of these comparisons would stop being trustworthy?

widget.prompt: A pizza is split into 3 equal parts. What do you call each slice?

options.label: a third
options.feedback: Correct — three equal parts, so each one is a third of the whole.

options.label: a half
options.feedback: A half means the whole was split into TWO equal parts, but this one was split into 3.

options.label: a fourth
options.feedback: A fourth names one of four equal parts, and nothing here was cut into four.

widget.prompt: Which is smaller: a half or a fourth?

options.label: a fourth
options.feedback: Correct — the whole is fixed, so the fraction with more pieces has smaller pieces.

options.label: a half
options.feedback: a half is not the smaller one here — cutting a whole into more pieces makes each piece smaller.

options.label: they're the same size
options.feedback: They differ: the same whole cut into more pieces gives smaller pieces every time.
